openingProblem.problem: Weimar democracy lasted fourteen years. West German democracy, founded in 1949 by many of the same generation, survived a narrow start, a former Nazi chancellor, student revolt and terrorism, and in 1990 absorbed East Germany. Why did Germany's second democracy prove so durable?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: what made West German democracy durable?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Chancellor democracy: the Adenauer era, 1949–1963
chunks.body:
Konrad Adenauer governed West Germany for fourteen years. The Basic Law helped him: because the Bundestag could remove a chancellor only by electing a successor, strong chancellors could govern for long periods. Adenauer used this position so forcefully that his rule was called **"chancellor democracy"**, a term, Geoff Layton notes, read positively or negatively depending on one's politics.

His foreign policy tied West Germany to the West. He secured membership of the Council of Europe in 1951 and helped create the European Coal and Steel Community in 1952. On **5 May 1955** West Germany regained its sovereignty and joined NATO, and a new army, the Bundeswehr, was created with conscription. Towards the East, Adenauer was unbending: under the **Hallstein Doctrine** of 1955, Bonn refused relations with any state that recognised East Germany, except the Soviet Union.

At home the **CDU** became a new kind of German party. It drew Catholics and Protestants, rural and urban voters, employers and workers. In Judt's phrase, the CDU "colonized the issues". Its vote almost doubled between 1949 and 1957, when it won more than half the votes cast. The opposition SPD, led by Kurt Schumacher, opposed Adenauer's Western policy and demanded a united, neutral Germany; its vote stagnated. The party system narrowed: from 1953 parties with less than 5 per cent of the vote were excluded from parliament, and in 1956 the Constitutional Court banned the Communist Party. Adenauer also courted the millions of expellees from the East, avoiding direct criticism of the German past.

The era ended badly. In the **Spiegel Affair** of 1962 the government, with Adenauer's authorisation, arrested the publisher of the news magazine *Der Spiegel* after it criticised defence policy. Even the conservative *Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung* called it "an embarrassment to our democracy". Adenauer stood down in 1963 and was succeeded by Ludwig Erhard.

This mattered because Adenauer's long rule gave the new democracy stability and Western security, which meant that West Germans came to associate democracy with prosperity and order, though at the cost of silence about the past.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The CDU became a broad people's party.
The party system narrowed around the centre.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Critics opposed the 5 per cent rule and party bans.

howItGetsAsked: Analyse the role of Konrad Adenauer in the development of West German democracy between 1949 and 1963.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Adenauer stabilised West German democracy by giving it strong government and Western security.
useItInAnEssay.prove: He won four elections up to 1961, led West Germany into NATO in 1955, and by 1957 the CDU/CSU won more than half the vote.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that democracy became associated with prosperity and security, so extremist parties lost ground.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, his style was called 'chancellor democracy', and in the Spiegel Affair of 1962 his government arrested a publisher for criticising defence policy.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Adenauer therefore secured democracy's stability more than its liberal culture.

chunks.title: Opposition renewed: Bad Godesberg and the Grand Coalition, 1959–1969
chunks.body:
For a decade the Social Democrats seemed unable to compete. In **1959**, at their congress at **Bad Godesberg**, a new generation of leaders abandoned the party's commitment to Marxism. The new programme accepted the free market ("The totalitarian directed economy destroys freedom") and the Western Alliance, and turned the SPD into a cross-class people's party (*Volkspartei*).

The change worked. Improved results in 1961 and 1965 led in 1966 to a **"grand coalition"** of CDU/CSU and SPD, with the Social Democrats, led by Willy Brandt, in government for the first time since Weimar. But the price was high. The new chancellor, chosen in December 1966, was **Kurt-Georg Kiesinger**, who had been a member of the Nazi Party for twelve years. With both big parties in government, there was almost no parliamentary opposition, and, Judt argues, a space opened *outside* parliament for a new generation of radicals.

That generation was angry about the past. The Eichmann trial of 1961 and the Frankfurt **Auschwitz trials** of 1963–65, with 273 witnesses, brought Nazi crimes to public attention. In 1967 Alexander and Margarete Mitscherlich argued that West Germany's official condemnation of Nazism had never been matched by individual acceptance of responsibility. The student movement of the late 1960s, the "extra-parliamentary Left", accused the Bonn Republic of hiding its founders' past. The film-maker Fassbinder complained that "our democracy was decreed for the Western occupation zone, we didn't fight for it ourselves".

In **1969** the SPD under Brandt formed a coalition with the Free Democrats. For the first time since 1949 the Christian Democrats were in opposition. Power had changed hands peacefully.

This mattered because the SPD's acceptance of the Federal Republic's basic choices made a change of government possible, which meant that West German democracy proved it could survive the defeat of its founding party.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Bad Godesberg made the SPD electable.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Many in the SPD remained unhappy with the EEC.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Grand Coalition weakened parliamentary opposition.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It brought the SPD into government for the first time since Weimar.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Bad Godesberg was the turning point that made a peaceful change of government possible.
useItInAnEssay.prove: In 1959 the SPD abandoned Marxism and accepted the free market and the Western Alliance; it entered government in 1966 and led it from 1969.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that both main parties accepted the Federal Republic's basic choices, so power could change hands without threatening the system.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Judt argues that once the SPD joined the government, a space opened outside parliament for radicals.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Bad Godesberg therefore strengthened democracy in parliament while helping to create opposition outside it.

chunks.title: Ostpolitik and terrorism, 1969–1982
chunks.body:
Brandt's government changed West Germany's policy towards the East. With his adviser Egon Bahr, he pursued **Ostpolitik**, "change through rapprochement". Brandt dropped the claim that East Germany was illegitimate, speaking instead of "one German nation, two German states". Treaties with Moscow and Warsaw in 1970 accepted the post-war frontiers; a four-power agreement on Berlin followed in 1971, and a **Basic Treaty** with East Germany was ratified in 1973. In Warsaw Brandt knelt at the memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto, and he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. In 1972 the SPD became the largest party in parliament for the first time. Contacts across the border grew: phone calls from West to East rose from half a million in 1969 to some forty million twenty years later. But reunification faded as a political goal: from the mid-1970s, never more than 1 per cent of West Germans called it the most important question.

At home, democracy faced its most violent challenge. The **Red Army Fraction** (the Baader-Meinhof Group) set out to destroy the Federal Republic by force. Between 1970 and 1978 it killed 28 people and took 162 hostages, and in 1977 it murdered the industrialist Hans Martin Schleyer, the Attorney General Siegfried Buback and the banker Jürgen Ponto. The state responded firmly: in 1972 Brandt's government introduced the *Berufsverbot*, excluding people judged hostile to the constitution from public employment, which critics feared would lead to censorship. Judt concludes that the terrorists failed, as did the neo-Nazi Right, whose bomb at the 1980 Munich Oktoberfest killed 13 people: neither destabilised the Republic.

Brandt resigned in 1974 after a spy scandal. His successor, **Helmut Schmidt**, kept to the line of Ostpolitik, as did the Christian Democrat **Helmut Kohl**, who became chancellor in 1982.

This mattered because West Germany both reduced tension with the East and withstood terrorism without abandoning democracy, which meant that the Federal Republic emerged from the 1970s more secure than its critics had feared.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It accepted the division of Germany.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Terrorism failed to destabilise the Republic.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Berufsverbot raised fears for civil liberties.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Ostpolitik succeeded in normalising relations with the East, at the price of accepting division.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Treaties with Moscow and Warsaw in 1970 and the Basic Treaty with the GDR in 1973 accepted the post-war frontiers, and phone calls between the two Germanies rose from half a million in 1969 to forty million twenty years later.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that human contacts grew and fears of West German revanchism eased, so even Kohl kept the policy.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the GDR gained international recognition, and from the mid-1970s fewer than 1 per cent of West Germans saw unification as the most important question.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Ostpolitik was therefore a success in reducing tension, but it seemed to make division permanent.

chunks.title: New parties and unification, 1982–1990
chunks.body:
By the 1980s the party system was changing. The **Greens**, a movement of environmentalists, pacifists and others, won 5.6 per cent of the vote and twenty-seven seats in the federal election of **1983**, entering parliament for the first time. By 1985 they were governing the state of Hesse in coalition with the SPD. The 5 per cent rule, designed to keep small extremist parties out, now let a new democratic party in once it reached the threshold.

Helmut Kohl, chancellor since 1982, was at first cautious when the Berlin Wall opened in November 1989. On 28 November he presented a *five-year* programme of steps towards unity. But as East Germans continued to flee west, Kohl accelerated. In the East German elections of **March 1990** the CDU-led "Alliance for Germany" won 48 per cent of the vote on a promise of unification. A monetary, economic and social union took effect on **1 July 1990**, bringing the Deutsche Mark to the East. On 23 August the East German parliament voted to join the Federal Republic, and on **3 October 1990** the GDR ceased to exist, acceding under Article 23 of the Basic Law.

Unification needed the consent of the four victorious powers. In the "4+2" talks of 1990 the USA backed Kohl, and the **Treaty on the Final Settlement with Respect to Germany**, signed in Moscow on 12 September 1990, recognised Germany's borders, ended four-power status in Berlin and allowed a united Germany to remain in NATO.

This mattered because East Germany joined the Federal Republic under its existing constitution, which meant that the democracy built in the West after 1949 became the democracy of all Germany.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Greens showed the system could absorb new movements.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The 5 per cent rule was criticised.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Kohl drove the pace of unification.

howItGetsAsked: To what extent was Helmut Kohl responsible for German unification between 1989 and 1990?
To what extent was the Basic Law the main reason for the stability of West German democracy between 1949 and 1969?

useItInAnEssay.claim: Kohl was responsible for the speed and form of unification, though not for the opportunity.
useItInAnEssay.prove: After presenting a five-year programme on 28 November 1989, he accelerated; the Alliance for Germany won 48 per cent in March 1990, and the GDR acceded on 3 October 1990.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that unification took place within the Federal Republic's Basic Law, so West German democracy was extended to the East.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, unification depended on the collapse of the GDR and on international consent, secured by US backing in the 4+2 talks.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Kohl was therefore responsible for how and when Germany united, but not for why it became possible.

segments.text: The Basic Law was the foundation of West German stability, but not its main cause.
The constructive vote of no confidence allowed strong chancellors such as Adenauer to govern for long periods, and from 1953 the 5 per cent rule kept splinter parties out.

The Basic Law was therefore necessary but not sufficient: stability came from voters and parties accepting democracy.

The Moscow and Warsaw treaties of 1970 accepted the post-war frontiers, and the Basic Treaty with the GDR was ratified in 1973.
This meant that fears of West German revanchism eased and contacts between the Germanies grew, so Brandt won the 1972 election and the Nobel Peace Prize.
However, the GDR gained international recognition, and from the mid-1970s fewer than 1 per cent of West Germans saw unification as the main question.
Ostpolitik was therefore successful by its own aims, which were normalisation, not unification.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the reasons for, and the results of, the SPD's Bad Godesberg programme between 1959 and 1969.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and which result was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: The SPD adopted the Bad Godesberg programme because its old Marxist and neutralist programme kept losing to the CDU; the result was entry into government in 1966 and leadership of it in 1969.

arguments.claim: Result: the SPD in power in 1969.

modelPlan.counter: Judt argues that joining the government cost the SPD the far Left.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which result mattered most? The peaceful change of government in 1969.

segments.text: The SPD changed its programme because its old one could not win.
Its vote stagnated in 1953 and 1957, so in 1959 at Bad Godesberg it abandoned Marxism and accepted the free market and the Western Alliance.
This meant that it could appeal beyond the working class, so its results improved in 1961 and 1965 and it entered government in 1966.
However, Judt argues that once the SPD joined the Grand Coalition, a space opened for radicals outside parliament.
The most significant result was therefore the SPD–FDP government of 1969, which proved power could change hands peacefully.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the role of Konrad Adenauer in the development of West German democracy between 1949 and 1963.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: Which contribution mattered most, and its costs

modelPlan.thesis: Adenauer's main contribution was stability, through long, strong government, Western integration and a broad CDU; but his 'chancellor democracy' and the Spiegel Affair showed authoritarian limits.

arguments.claim: The CDU as a people's party.
Limits: the past and the Spiegel Affair.

modelPlan.counter: Adenauer avoided criticising the German past to win expellee votes.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which contribution mattered most? Stability through Western integration.

segments.text: Adenauer's central role was to make democracy stable and Western.
He led West Germany into NATO in 1955, won four elections up to 1961, and by 1957 the CDU/CSU won more than half the vote.
This meant that democracy became associated with security and prosperity, so nationalist and communist parties declined.
However, his rule was called 'chancellor democracy', he avoided criticising the Nazi past, and his government abused power in the Spiegel Affair of 1962.
Adenauer therefore secured democracy's stability, while its liberal culture developed after him.

essayQuestions.text: To what extent was Helmut Kohl responsible for German unification between 1989 and 1990?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.judgement: How far did the outcome depend on him?

modelPlan.thesis: Kohl was responsible for the speed and form of unification, accelerating from a five-year plan to accession within a year; but the opportunity came from the GDR's collapse and international consent, especially US backing.

arguments.claim: The March 1990 election and monetary union.
The framework of the Basic Law.

modelPlan.counter: Kohl was at first cautious, proposing a five-year programme on 28 November 1989.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: How far did it depend on him? The timing and form, yes; the opportunity, no.

segments.text: Kohl was largely responsible for how quickly and in what form Germany united.
After presenting a five-year programme on 28 November 1989 he accelerated: the Alliance for Germany won 48 per cent in March 1990 and monetary union took effect on 1 July.
This meant that East Germany joined the Federal Republic under Article 23, so unification came on West German terms on 3 October 1990.
However, unification also required international consent, secured in the Treaty on the Final Settlement with US support.
Kohl was therefore responsible for the form and pace of unification, but not for the conditions that made it possible.

essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the threat posed by terrorism to democracy in West Germany and Spain between 1970 and 1987.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences throughout
decodeKey.judgement: How serious was each threat, and how did each democracy respond?

modelPlan.thesis: Terrorism failed to destroy democracy in both states, but the threats differed: West Germany's RAF had no defined goals and little popular base, whereas Spain's ETA fought for Basque independence and killed far more people; both governments responded with measures that raised doubts about civil liberties, more seriously in Spain.

arguments.claim: Similarity: responses that raised doubts about liberty.

modelPlan.counter: Judt calls the Spanish response 'arguably a remarkably moderate response' in the circumstances.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which threat was greater? ETA's, because it had a cause with regional support and killed far more people.

segments.text: Terrorism threatened democracy in both West Germany and Spain, but ETA was the greater danger.
The RAF killed 28 people between 1970 and 1978, whereas ETA killed 181 people in 1979–80 alone, after assassinating Franco's prime minister in 1973.
This meant that ETA, fighting for Basque independence, posed a lasting challenge to the new Spanish state, while the RAF, with no defined goals, failed to disrupt the Federal Republic.
However, both democracies answered with measures that worried liberals: West Germany's Berufsverbot of 1972 was legal, whereas Spain's GAL killed twenty-six ETA operatives illegally in 1983–87.
Both democracies therefore survived terrorism, but Spain's younger democracy was more seriously tested and more seriously compromised by its response.
